Telemetry and audit log improvements (SOC 2 artifacts)

Dedicated vs hosted surge protection and cost tradeoffs

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-27
Time: 15:00 UTC (54m)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Arjun Patel (Redwood SE); Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Evan Ross (TruRange - Head of Platform); Priya Nair (TruRange - SRE Manager); Marcus Liu (TruRange - CTO)
---
Auto-summary (brief): Intake for escalation playbook after last week's production fallthrough. Focus on immediate mitigations, telemetry gaps, and an agreed pilot to validate runbook steps under load.

00:00 - 00:28 Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for jumping on, um this is Maya from Redwood. Arjun and Lena are with me. Evan, Priya, Marcus — thanks for your time, I know this is still fresh, so we want to make this practical, not a repeat of the postmortem slides.

00:30 - 01:05 Evan Ross: Yeah, appreciate it. We — the incident last Thursday hit a bunch of customers and, uh, exposed a couple of weak spots in our fallthroughs. We had two routes where the fallback loop made failures worse, so we're looking for concrete, operator-friendly steps.

01:10 - 01:45 Arjun Patel: Sorry to hear that — can you briefly state the sequence you saw? We have some initial hypotheses around KV cache cold-start and a cascade from the larger model to the smaller variant triggering a token storm.

01:47 - 02:35 Priya Nair: Sure. Timeline in short: around 08:12 UTC we got a spike of long-context requests, tokens per request jumped, the primary model got overloaded and head-of-line built up. The system auto-fell back to the smaller model but it seems the fallback wasn't idempotent and clients retried aggressively. Also KV cache miss rates spiked so latency doubled; that killed some of our canaries.

02:37 - 03:15 Marcus Liu: Important note — we were on Redwood Hosted for prod, not dedicated capacity. We have the dedicated project in eval but not yet live. So there's a capacity and multi-tenant unpredictability question.

03:20 - 04:00 Maya Chen: Thanks. Okay, so three threads: behavior of the fallback loop, KV cache warming and miss patterns, and the hosted vs dedicated capacity decision. We'll aim to map concrete guardrails for each.

04:10 - 05:00 Evan Ross: From the customer side we also need better audit-level traces — token-level cost per request, and who triggered what rollback. Our security/compliance team is asking for audit logs that tie to SSO/SAML users and request IDs. We couldn't reconstruct the sequence quickly.

05:05 - 06:00 Lena Ortiz: Understood. We can share an excerpt of our audit logs and SOC 2 artifact to show what we can surface today; but there are known gaps in token-level tracing for multi-model fallbacks. We'll include a gap map in the runbook draft.

06:05 - 06:48 Priya Nair: Another question — when we used the smaller model fallback, the cost seemed to spike because the retry pattern increased tokens overall. Is there a recommended throttling layer at the client or at the Redwood router?

06:50 - 07:40 Arjun Patel: We recommend a couple of approaches: request-side throttles, router-level queue depth limits, and introducing a short cooldown (backoff) on fallback responses. Also we can route to a 'degraded mode' model that returns truncated responses rather than full re-generation which uses fewer tokens. But that changes UX.

07:45 - 09:10 Evan Ross: Truncated responses might be acceptable for a certain percentage of requests during surges. We need a policy though — who decides the tradeoff? We have product owners and we need a policy that can be automated — like degrade to summary-only for >X tokens or >Y latency.

09:15 - 10:02 Maya Chen: Right. That's why runbook decisions should include thresholds (latency > 1.2s p95, token count > 8k) and automatic triggers with explicit owners. If automated, also include canary window and manual override.

10:05 - 11:10 Marcus Liu: On telemetry: can Redwood include request-level IDs and propagate our internal trace IDs into Redwood logs so we can stitch traces end-to-end? We tried tracing but IDs got lost crossing the API boundary.

11:12 - 12:00 Arjun Patel: We can add a header pass-through that preserves trace IDs, and we'll confirm field names. There is a limit on header size and some sanitization that can affect it, but it's doable. We'll add that to the RFC for the runbook.

12:05 - 13:20 Priya Nair: Also, the KV cache behavior — is it possible to pre-warm the KV for known heavy keys during deployments? During the incident we saw a cold cache after a model switch.

13:22 - 14:10 Arjun Patel: Yes, KV warm-up strategies exist. We suggested two: prefix warm-up (push commonly seen prefixes) and scheduled synthetic warm-ups right after a code deploy or after fallback events. We'll simulate the warm-up for your sample traffic. Note: synthetic warm-up costs tokens during warm-up but can avoid a bigger outage.

14:12 - 15:05 Evan Ross: What about batching — we saw that batch sizes collapsed during the spike. Is continuous batching contributing to head-of-line blocking?

15:10 - 16:00 Arjun Patel: Continuous batching helps throughput but can hurt latency if queuing isn't throttled. We can tune batch windows and prioritize small-latency routes. Also, the router can be configured to hold a small fast-path for low-latency calls. We'll propose parameters.

16:05 - 17:20 Marcus Liu: There's also the matter of model quantization changes the inference speed; your compilation picks kernels — can a kernel selection flip cause transient slowdowns?

17:22 - 18:00 Arjun Patel: Kernel selection can change perf characteristics; we have heuristics to avoid dynamic recompile in the hot path, but if there's a sudden model switch or sequence length jump we sometimes hit a less-optimal kernel. For hosted mode we manage that, for dedicated we give you more predictability.

18:05 - 19:10 Priya Nair: We do want to know the concrete delta between hosted and dedicated for our workload — both latency p95 and cost per 1M tokens, roughly. That will factor into our budget and decision timeline.

19:12 - 20:00 Maya Chen: We'll include a cost-latency delta with your sample traffic in the bench test. Quick numbers offhand: dedicated typically reduces 95th latency by 20-40% for long-context workloads and reduces variability; cost depends heavily on reserved capacity commit and burst patterns. We'll put conservative estimates in the runbook.

20:05 - 21:30 Evan Ross: Back to escalation ownership — during the incident there was confusion who owned the 'fallthrough' policy: our app SRE or Redwood ops? We need a clear handoff in runbook steps: who flips the switch, who runs the canary, who notifies customers.

21:32 - 22:20 Lena Ortiz: Good point — runbook will have roles and responsibilities: Customer on-call (TruRange SRE) owns app-side throttles and can trigger manual overrides; Redwood SE/ops will own router-level toggles and model variant activation; CSM (Lena) owns comms and customer notifications. We'll put specific contact escalation matrix and Slack channels into the draft.

22:22 - 24:00 Priya Nair: For compliance we also need to know where request payloads and logs live — do backups or traces include PII? How long are they retained? We run in EU region for some customers and need residency information.

24:05 - 25:20 Maya Chen: We'll share our data residency options (hosted region mapping) and retention defaults. For PII you can mask at client side or request us to enable redaction; we also support KMS integrations for key control in Private deployments. We'll attach the security doc.

25:25 - 27:00 Marcus Liu: Another edge case: the fallback triggered because the primary model returned a slow NACK which clients retried — is there an idempotency or request token to prevent re-generation on retries?

27:05 - 28:10 Arjun Patel: We'll add an idempotency key recommendation: if the client sends a persistent request_id we can dedupe at the Redwood router for a short window. That reduces duplicate token consumption on retries. We'll document header names and TTLs.

28:15 - 29:40 Evan Ross: Could Redwood expose a 'degraded-summary' mode? We mentioned truncation but a summary-only model variant that costs less and responds quickly might be better than partial re-generation.

29:45 - 31:00 Arjun Patel: Yes, we can propose a degraded variant — either a specialized smaller model optimized for summaries or a policy to limit max tokens. We'll include recommended quality thresholds and guardrails for fallback percentage.

31:05 - 33:00 Priya Nair: For the pilot bench test, can Redwood run a synthetic spike that matches our observed token distribution — long tails and bursts — and show both latency and token-cost outcomes for hosted vs dedicated vs degraded model fallback?

33:05 - 34:10 Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll need your traffic export (anonymized) and a list of routes to include. Arjun will run the bench and Mel from infra will help if we need dedicated cluster quotas. We'll aim for a reproducible test plan.

34:12 - 35:20 Marcus Liu: On the customer comms side, we need a template for status updates and for the customer-facing write-up. We don't want to be reactive again. Can Redwood supply a language template for different severity levels?

35:22 - 36:00 Lena Ortiz: Yes, CSM can provide a template library and we'll co-author a post-incident public note. We'll include recommended timing (initial ack in 15-30m, triage update in 60m, full postmortem within 72h).

36:05 - 37:40 Evan Ross: Are there quick mitigations we can enable now while the runbook is being drafted? E.g., set a global cap on fallback percentage to 10% and enforce client-side backoff.

37:45 - 38:30 Arjun Patel: We can push a temporary router rule to cap fallback activations per minute for your account; this is an emergency throttle we use for mitigation. I'll include a safe command and rollback instructions.

38:35 - 39:20 Priya Nair: Good. Also would like a mechanism to force a cold-start protection window after a deploy to avoid simultaneous model resets — like a staggered restart.

39:25 - 40:10 Arjun Patel: We'll recommend a staged rollout: 10% canary, then 30%, then full with KV warming between steps. We'll include steps to abort and options to revert quickly.

40:15 - 41:30 Marcus Liu: We also want to understand the alerting signals — which metrics should trigger runbook steps? Token-per-request p95, request latency p95, KV miss rate, fallback rate per minute, and queued request depth sound right. Any other?

41:32 - 42:20 Maya Chen: Add error rate on model responses and early NACKs. We'll provide a recommended list with thresholds tuned to your baseline.

42:25 - 44:00 Evan Ross: One more thing — legal asked about evidence for SLA credits if a fallthrough is due to Redwood's capacity; what artifacts will Redwood provide for dispute resolution?

44:05 - 45:00 Lena Ortiz: We can provide request-level timelines, capacity usage graphs, and the audit logs we discussed. SLA disputes are handled per contract; we have a standard pack of artifacts we share for investigations. We'll add that to the runbook as an evidence checklist.

45:05 - 46:10 Priya Nair: For the bench test, please include both wall-clock latency and token cost and an estimated per-user cost impact so we can reason about product tradeoffs.

46:15 - 47:05 Arjun Patel: Will do. We'll also include a KB of recommended QoS settings for clients (max tokens allowed, retry backoff, idempotency TTL).

47:10 - 48:00 Evan Ross: Timeline check — we want the runbook and gap map by next week if possible. Can Redwood meet that?

48:05 - 49:00 Maya Chen: Yes, Arjun and I will have a candidate runbook and gap map to you by 2026-12-01. Bench test scheduling next week — Lena will coordinate.

49:05 - 50:30 Marcus Liu: Ok, thanks — any blockers on data sharing? We'll anonymize payloads but need a secure upload method.

50:35 - 51:20 Lena Ortiz: We'll send a secure S3 link and instructions for encryption and key exchange. For PII, please mark fields to redact; we'll provide a checklist.

51:25 - 52:40 Evan Ross: Sounds good. Quick call-out: competitor approach — we did a bench with Infracloud two months ago and they recommended aggressive client-side throttles; Anthropic did a hybrid dedicated approach. Curious to see Redwood's hybrid suggestion.

52:45 - 53:30 Maya Chen: We'll include hybrid patterns — short term hosted throttles + long-term dedicated capacity with reserved buffers.

53:32 - 54:00 Maya Chen (closing): Thanks everyone — recap: Arjun will draft runbook and technical gaps, Lena handles scheduling and comms templates, Maya will send security artifacts, Priya/Evan will share anonymized traces. We'll meet again after bench test. We'll drop the runbook link and next steps into CRM.

---
Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (Redwood dedicated sometimes transcribed as 'Redwood dedicate'), technical names occasionally inconsistent (KV cache spelled 'K V cache' or 'kv-cache'); filler words (um/uh) present.
questions: What exact thresholds should runbook use for p95 latency and fallback rate?
Can Redwood annotate logs with our internal trace IDs?
Which model variant is preferred for degraded-summary mode?
